teacherGuide.overview: Efua starts a small groundnut-cake business and is tempted by a classmate’s shortcuts. The story joins real arithmetic (cost, revenue, profit) to a choice about honesty, and shows that a trustworthy reputation is part of a business’s value.
learningGoals: Work out cost, income and profit from a simple business and check a claim against the numbers.
Explain why trust and honesty matter to customers and to a business over time.
Infer a character’s reasoning and the meaning of a metaphor ("customers are like a garden").
Apply the story to a real choice in the learner’s own life.

beforeReading: Ask: "Have you ever bought something from a school-gate seller? What made you go back, or not?"
Pre-teach: profit, cost, trust. Write "profit = money in − money spent" on the board.
whileReading: After page 3, pause for the profit activity: check every learner can get to eight cedis.
After page 6, ask for predictions before reading on (the prediction activity).
After page 7, let learners check Kwabena’s "twice the profit" claim with Efua’s numbers.
afterReading: Put the events in order, then retell the story in three sentences.
Have learners recalculate with the final recipe: cost 65 pesewas per pack, selling at one cedi.
discussion: Was Kwabena a bad person, or someone giving poor advice? How do you know?
Efua made less profit on some days. What did she gain that the sums alone do not show?
How was selling leftover cakes at half price different from calling them fresh?
What does "Customers are like a garden" mean? Can you think of another comparison?
reflection: Think of a time you were tempted to take a shortcut. What did you do, and what would you do now?
What do people say about you when you are not there? How could you build a reputation you are proud of?
Where in your own life (school, home, a small job, a class project) does honesty cost you something in the short term and pay off later?
Who is your "Auntie Dede", someone whose advice you trust? What makes them trustworthy?

mathsExtension.task: Efua sells all 20 packs at 1 cedi each. Cost 12 cedis. What is the profit?
On Monday she sold 14 packs of the 20 she made. What was her profit?
mathsExtension.answer: 14 − 12 = 2 cedis (the six unsold packs were already paid for).

mathsExtension.task: With fewer groundnuts, 20 packs cost 9 cedis. What is the profit if all 20 sell? How much more than 8 cedis is that?
mathsExtension.answer: 20 − 9 = 11 cedis, which is 3 cedis more. Kwabena promised "twice", which would be 16.

mathsExtension.task: The honest recipe costs 65 pesewas a pack. What do 25 packs cost, and what is the profit if all sell at 1 cedi?
mathsExtension.answer: 25 × 65 = 1,625 pesewas = 16.25 cedis. Profit 25 − 16.25 = 8.75 cedis, more than the original 8 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Challenge: Efua sells 5 half-price packs (50 pesewas each) and 20 full-price packs a day. Cost: 16.25 cedis for 25 packs. What is the profit?
mathsExtension.answer: Income 20 + 2.50 = 22.50 cedis. Profit 22.50 − 16.25 = 6.25 cedis. Honest half-price selling costs a little, and still earns trust.

support: Use whole-cedi numbers only (pages 3 and 7) and a number line for subtraction.

stretch: Ask learners to design their own small business and cost it, including how they would handle leftovers honestly.

factCheck.claim: The Big Bang was an expansion of space everywhere from an extremely hot, dense state ~13.8 billion years ago, not an explosion from a single point into pre-existing empty space.
factCheck.explanation: General relativity and cosmological observations (Planck collaboration, 2018) show metric expansion of space itself with an age of 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years.
factCheck.analogyNote: The rising raisin-bread analogy illustrates uniform expansion between unbound galaxy clusters, but teachers should note that galaxies themselves stay bound by gravity and real space has no external "oven" or boundary.
factCheck.reference: NASA Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) & ESA Planck Mission Cosmology Overview; IAU Office of Astronomy for Education.

factCheck.claim: Redshift of distant galaxies, the Cosmic Microwave Background (released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang), and light-element abundances are the primary observational pillars of Big Bang cosmology.
factCheck.explanation: Cosmological redshift stretches photon wavelengths as the scale factor increases; recombination at ~380,000 years released the CMB now observed at 2.725 K.
factCheck.reference: Peebles, P. J. E. (2020), Principles of Physical Cosmology; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center CMB Education Resources.

factCheck.claim: What happened at t = 0 (the Planck epoch) and the exact nature of dark matter and dark energy remain unresolved scientific questions.
factCheck.explanation: Current physics requires a unified theory of quantum gravity to describe t = 0, and dark matter/dark energy remain active areas of empirical investigation.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Lake Bosomtwe in the Ashanti Region, this story helps Upper Primary learners distinguish between respected cultural oral traditions (how communities relate to and conserve a sacred place) and empirical geological evidence (how a Pleistocene meteorite impact carved the crater 1.07 million years ago and preserved a million-year West African climate archive).
learningGoals: Explain how a meteorite impact formed the Lake Bosomtwe crater approximately 1.07 million years ago.
Identify real geological evidence for an impact crater: circular rim, shocked quartz in breccia, and Ivory Coast tektites.
Explain how annual sediment layers at the bottom of a closed (endorheic) lake record past climate changes.
Respectfully distinguish traditional cultural stories and conservation practices from testable geological explanations.

beforeReading: Locate the Ashanti Region and Lake Bosomtwe (about 30 km south-east of Kumasi) on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "Have you ever seen a photograph of craters on the Moon? Could a rock from space make a crater on Earth too?"
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to discuss how the traditional rule against iron boats and loud motors also helps protect the lake from oil pollution and overfishing.
Pause after page 8 to trace the direction from Lake Bosomtwe westward to Côte d’Ivoire where tektites landed.
afterReading: Compare the two questions: "How did people come to revere and care for Lake Bosomtwe?" (cultural history) and "What physical process carved the 10.5 km rock basin?" (geological science).
discussion: Why did scientists rule out the idea that Lake Bosomtwe is a volcanic crater?
How can tiny crystals inside a rock or glassy pebbles in Côte d’Ivoire act as clues to an event that happened over a million years ago?
Why are the mud layers at the bottom of Lake Bosomtwe compared to pages in a history book?
reflection: How can traditional community rules and modern environmental science work together to protect Ghana’s lakes and forests today?

mathsExtension.task: The outer crater rim around Lake Bosomtwe is about 10.5 km wide, while the water surface today is about 8.5 km wide. What is the difference between the crater rim width and the water width?

mathsExtension.answer: 1,000 metres = 1 kilometre; 500 metres is 1/2 (0.5) of a kilometre.

support: Use a bowl and a cup of water to show what a "closed lake" (endorheic basin) means: water enters as rain and leaves only by evaporation.
stretch: Write a short field report explaining three clues you would look for as a geologist to tell an impact crater apart from a volcano.

culturalNotes: Lake Bosomtwe is sacred in Ashanti tradition. The oral tradition of the hunter Akora Bompe and his dog from Asaman following an antelope (twe) is presented respectfully as cultural heritage, never confused with geological age.
The traditional wooden plank craft is called a padua, propelled with flat wooden hand pads.
localiseThis: Connect to any notable rock formations, hills, rivers, or sacred groves in your own district and discuss both their cultural story and geological origin.

whatWeKnow: Lake Bosomtwe occupies a 10.5 km wide meteorite impact crater formed approximately 1.07 million years ago in crystalline Birimian rocks.
Shocked quartz in suevite breccia and radiometrically matched Ivory Coast tektites confirm an extraterrestrial hypervelocity impact.
Deep sediment cores drilled in 2004 (ICDP) preserve over 1 million years of West African monsoon and Sahara dust history.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Scientists continue analysing microscopic pollen, charcoal, and chemical isotopes in the deep lake cores to understand how rapid climate shifts affected early human habitats in West Africa.
Hydrologists are actively studying how modern warming and land-use changes around the rim affect the lake’s water balance and native cichlid fish species.

investigation.title: Model an Impact Crater in a Tray
materials: A wide shallow basin or cardboard tray
Dry gari, cornflour, or clean fine sand (about 4 cm deep)
A thin dusting of cocoa powder or dark soil on top
Two or three smooth pebbles or marbles of different sizes
A ruler
steps: Spread a 4 cm layer of gari or fine sand smoothly in the tray and sprinkle a very thin dark layer of cocoa powder or dark soil on top.
Drop a small pebble from shoulder height straight down into the tray and measure the width of the circular crater rim.
Observe where the lighter lower layer was thrown outward (like tektites and ejecta rays).
Gently toss a pebble at a slight angle and notice that the crater still forms a nearly round bowl!
investigation.whatToNotice: Even when a pebble hits at a moderate angle, the shock wave pushes material outward in all directions to make a circular rim with a raised edge.
investigation.safetyNote: Drop pebbles gently downward into the tray placed on the ground; stand back slightly so sand or powder does not splash near eyes, and wash hands afterwards.

factCheck.claim: Lake Bosomtwe was formed approximately 1.07 million years ago by a meteorite impact producing a ~10.5 km crater.
factCheck.explanation: Argon-argon dating of Ivory Coast tektites and impact glasses, combined with geophysical and drilling studies of the Bosomtwe structure, establish an impact age of 1.07 Myr.
factCheck.reference: Koeberl, C., Milkereit, B., Overpeck, J. T., Scholz, C. A., Amoako, P. Y. O., Boamah, D., Danuor, S. et al. (2007). An international and multidisciplinary drilling project into a young complex impact structure: The 2004 Bosomtwe crater drilling project. Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 42(4–5), 483–511.

factCheck.claim: Shocked quartz in impact breccia and Ivory Coast tektites provide conclusive geological evidence of hypervelocity impact.
factCheck.explanation: Planar deformation features in quartz require shock pressures >5–10 GPa that volcanic processes on Earth cannot generate; Ivory Coast tektites have identical chemical and isotopic signatures to the Birimian target rocks at Bosomtwe.
factCheck.reference: Boamah, D., & Koeberl, C. (2003). Geology and geochemistry of shallow drill cores from the Bosomtwe impact crater, Ghana. Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 38(8), 1137–1159; UNESCO Biosphere Reserve Nomination Dossier for Lake Bosomtwe.

Contrast photosynthesis at the ocean surface with chemosynthesis at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

investigation.title: See How Water Depth Increases Pressure
materials: An empty 1.5-litre clear plastic water bottle
A ruler and marker
A compass point or nail (handled by the teacher)
Waterproof tape
A bucket or outdoor sink and water
steps: Have the teacher carefully poke three small, equal-sized pinholes in a vertical line down the side of the plastic bottle: one near the top (5 cm down), one in the middle (12 cm down), and one near the bottom (20 cm down).
Cover all three holes with a strip of tape and fill the bottle completely with water (leave the cap off).
Place the bottle at the edge of a table over a bucket or outdoors, peel off the tape all at once, and observe how far each stream of water shoots out horizontally.
investigation.whatToNotice: The stream from the bottom hole shoots out the farthest and fastest because there is a taller column of water pressing down above it—demonstrating how hydrostatic pressure increases with depth!
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should use a sharp point to make the pinholes in the plastic bottle; perform the water test outdoors or over a bucket so floors do not become slippery.

factCheck.claim: About three-quarters of deep pelagic marine organisms produce bioluminescence using luciferin and luciferase.

factCheck.reference: Martini, S., & Haddock, S. H. D. (2017). Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea demonstrates its predominance as an ecological trait. Scientific Reports, 7, 45750; NOAA Ocean Exploration — Bioluminescence and Deep-Sea Vents.

factCheck.claim: Hydrothermal vents host ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis, first discovered in 1977.

whatWeKnow: African elephants live in matriarchal family units where the oldest female retains decades of spatial memory for water and food routes.

investigation.title: Listen to Vibrations Through Solid Wood vs Air
materials: A long wooden classroom desk or table
Your fingertips or a wooden pencil with an eraser end
steps: Have one learner sit at one end of a long wooden desk and tap the wood very softly with a fingertip so their partner standing at the other end can barely hear it through the air.
Now have the partner rest one ear gently flat against the wooden desktop (or press their palm flat on the wood) while the first learner taps with the exact same gentle force.
Compare how clear the tap sounds and feels through the solid wood compared to through the air.
investigation.whatToNotice: Vibrations travel strongly through solid materials like wood and soil—similar to how elephants sense low seismic rumbles through the ground with their feet!
investigation.safetyNote: Tap only very gently with a fingertip or eraser—never bang hard while a classmate’s ear is resting on the desk.

factCheck.claim: Elephants communicate using low-frequency infrasound rumbles and detect seismic ground vibrations through their feet.
factCheck.explanation: Elephant vocalizations include fundamental frequencies of 14–35 Hz that propagate through air and ground; elephant foot pads contain Pacinian corpuscles and acoustic fat pads sensitive to seismic vibrations.
factCheck.reference: O’Connell-Rodwell, C. E. (2007). Keeping an "Ear" to the Ground: Seismic Communication in Elephants. Physiology, 22(4), 287–294; Cornell Lab of Ornithology — Elephant Listening Project.

factCheck.claim: Beehive fences deter elephants from crop fields because elephants fear honeybee stings around their eyes and inside their trunks.
factCheck.explanation: Field trials across Africa demonstrate that elephants actively avoid African honeybees (Apis mellifera scutellata) and emit specific alarm rumbles when hearing bee buzzes.
factCheck.reference: King, L. E., Douglas-Hamilton, I., & Vollrath, F. (2007). African elephants run from the sound of disturbed bees. Current Biology, 17(19), R832–R833; Save the Elephants — Elephants and Bees Project.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, this JHS 2–3 story demystifies black holes using clear physics: debunking the "cosmic vacuum cleaner" myth, explaining escape velocity and the event horizon, presenting four independent lines of observational evidence (stellar orbits around Sagittarius A*, X-ray accretion disks, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio imaging), and highlighting open questions in quantum gravity.

Define escape velocity and explain why light cannot escape from inside the event horizon.
Describe four real astronomical methods used to detect black holes (stellar orbits, accretion-disk X-rays, gravitational waves, and EHT shadow imaging).
Distinguish established relativistic physics from unresolved questions about quantum gravity and the interior of black holes.

whatWeKnow: Stellar-mass black holes form from the gravitational collapse of massive stars, and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) reside at the centres of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.
Outside the event horizon, a black hole’s gravitational field obeys Einstein’s general relativity (and approximates Newton’s law of gravitation at large distances).
Astronomers have verified black holes through stellar orbits (2020 Nobel Prize in Physics), gravitational waves (LIGO/Virgo, 2015), X-ray accretion disks, and EHT horizon-scale images (2019, 2022).
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Physicists do not yet have a complete, experimentally verified theory of quantum gravity to describe what replaces the classical "singularity" inside a black hole.
The black hole information paradox—how quantum information is preserved when a black hole slowly evaporates via Hawking radiation—remains an active theoretical question.
Astronomers are still investigating using the James Webb Space Telescope how the earliest supermassive black holes grew so rapidly in the young universe.

investigation.title: Model Gravity and Orbits on a Stretched Cloth
materials: A large plastic basin or bucket (or four students holding the corners of a stretchy cloth taut)
A piece of stretchy T-shirt fabric or lycra cloth
A heavy smooth stone or metal ball
Two or three small glass marbles
steps: Stretch the cloth smoothly and tightly across the top of the basin (or have four learners hold the edges tight and level).
Roll a small marble straight across the flat cloth and observe that it travels in a straight line.
Place the heavy stone in the middle so the cloth curves downward into a funnel, then roll the small marble sideways near the outer edge at a moderate speed so it curves in an orbit around the stone.
Now roll the marble very slowly or aim it closely at the steep central dip and observe how it spirals inward.
investigation.whatToNotice: At a safe distance with enough sideways speed, the marble orbits around the heavy mass without getting "sucked in"; only paths that pass too close or too slowly fall into the steep central well.
investigation.safetyNote: Hold the heavy stone carefully so it does not drop onto toes, and keep small marbles off the floor so nobody slips.

factCheck.claim: Replacing the Sun with a black hole of equal mass would not suck in the Earth; Earth would maintain its orbit.
factCheck.explanation: By Birkhoff’s theorem in general relativity (and Newton’s shell theorem), the external gravitational field at distances much greater than the Schwarzschild radius (r_s ≈ 3 km for 1 solar mass) is identical to that of the Sun.
factCheck.analogyNote: The stretched-cloth analogy helps visualise how mass curves spacetime, but teachers should clarify that real spacetime is 4-dimensional (not a 2D sheet) and balls on a cloth slow down due to friction, whereas space is nearly frictionless.
factCheck.reference: NASA Black Hole Safety & Myths FAQ; Thorne, K. S. (1994), Black Holes and Time Warps.

factCheck.claim: Sagittarius A* (~4 million solar masses) and M87* have been confirmed through stellar orbits, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio interferometry.
factCheck.explanation: Ghez et al. and Genzel et al. tracked star S2 orbiting Sgr A* (2020 Nobel Prize); LIGO detected binary black hole mergers in 2015 (GW150914); the EHT Collaboration published direct shadow images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022).
factCheck.reference: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019, 2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 & 2020 Scientific Background.

teacherGuide.overview: Designed for Primary 1–2 learners, this schoolyard story introduces practical observation and measurement (comparing temperatures in sun vs shade), explains in child-friendly terms how trees cool their surroundings through shade and transpiration/evaporation, and models environmental teamwork through tree planting and care.
learningGoals: Observe and compare temperatures in direct sunlight versus under tree shade.
Explain two ways trees help cool a compound: blocking direct solar rays (shade) and releasing moisture from leaves that evaporates (transpiration).
Identify what young saplings need to survive (water, soil, sunlight, mulch to hold moisture, and protection from browsing animals).
Work cooperatively with classmates to care for the school environment.

Ask learners: "Where do you like to stand during midday break on a very hot day? Why?"

Pause after page 6 and have learners blow gently on a damp hand to feel how evaporating water cools skin.

discussion: What happens to bare soil when the hot sun shines on it all day with no trees or grass?
Why did the children water the saplings early in the morning and put dry leaves (mulch) around the soil?
Why do young trees in Ghana often need a small fence or basket guard around them?
reflection: What is one thing you and your friends can do this week to care for plants or trees at school or at home?

mathsExtension.task: The temperature in the sun was 36 degrees and the temperature in the shade was 30 degrees. How many degrees cooler was the shade?
Team Green planted 4 saplings. If each sapling needs 2 cans of water in the morning, how many cans of water do they carry altogether?

support: Do the damp-hand cooling test in class: wet the back of one hand with a drop of clean water, keep the other hand dry, wave both gently, and feel which hand feels cooler.
stretch: Draw a labelled picture of a tree showing the roots drinking water, the trunk carrying it up, and the leaves making shade and cool air.

culturalNotes: Neem (Azadirachta indica) and mango trees are among the most common schoolyard and compound shade trees across Ghana; ampe is a beloved Ghanaian jumping and clapping game.
Kwame, Abena, and Akua are Akan day names.
localiseThis: Name the specific shade trees growing in your own school compound (such as neem, mango, acacia, rain tree, or almond tree).

whatWeKnow: Tree canopies intercept incoming solar radiation, reducing surface temperatures beneath them by several degrees Celsius compared to bare sunlit ground.
Trees absorb water through their roots and release water vapour through tiny leaf pores (stomata) in a process called transpiration, which absorbs heat energy and cools surrounding air.
Tree roots bind topsoil and reduce rainwater runoff and erosion on school compounds.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Urban foresters and climate scientists in West Africa are studying which native Ghanaian tree species cool towns best while surviving longer dry spells.

investigation.title: Compare Sun and Shade with Two Cups of Water
materials: Two identical plastic cups
Clean water from the same bucket or tap
A sunny spot and a shady spot under a tree or veranda
A classroom thermometer (or clean fingers to compare warmth)
steps: Fill both cups halfway with water from the same bucket so they start at the exact same temperature.
Place Cup A out in direct sunlight and Cup B in the shade under a tree for 30 minutes during morning lessons.
After 30 minutes, bring both cups together and measure the water temperature with a thermometer (or touch the outside of each cup to compare).
investigation.whatToNotice: Cup A from the direct sun feels noticeably warmer than Cup B from the shade, showing how shade blocks solar heat energy!
investigation.safetyNote: Use plastic cups (not breakable glass), and stay in the shade as much as possible when setting out and collecting the cups at midday.

factCheck.claim: Trees cool their surroundings both by blocking direct solar radiation (shade) and through evaporative cooling from transpiration.
factCheck.explanation: Canopy shading reduces surface radiant heating, while latent heat of vaporization during leaf transpiration cools ambient air temperature (typically 2–8 °C cooler surface/local feel depending on soil moisture and canopy density).
factCheck.reference: FAO Urban and Peri-Urban Forestry Guidelines; US EPA — Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands.

teacherGuide.overview: Set in Koforidua in the Eastern Region, this Upper Primary story integrates scientific observation, fair testing, data representation (bar graphs), verified arithmetic (addition, subtraction, and mean of 5-day rainfall data), and the foundational distinction between daily weather and long-term climate across Ghana’s ecological zones.
learningGoals: Explain why a rain gauge must have straight sides and be placed in an open site away from roofs and trees.
Read and interpret a 5-day rainfall dataset in millimetres, calculate the total (50 mm), range (18 mm − 0 mm), and mean (10 mm/day), and represent the data on a bar graph.
Clearly distinguish between daily weather and long-term climate (30+ year averages).
Describe how rainfall records help farmers and water managers in Ghana.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a big bucket and a narrow straight jar stand side by side in the open rain, will the water be deeper in the bucket, deeper in the jar, or the same depth?" (Wait to revisit after page 3!)

Pause after page 8 to verify the addition (12 + 0 + 18 + 6 + 14 = 50 mm) and division (50 ÷ 5 = 10 mm).
afterReading: Have every learner draw the 5-day bar graph in their exercise book with a ruler, labelling the horizontal axis (Monday to Friday) and the vertical axis (Rainfall in mm, counting by 2s from 0 to 20).
discussion: Why did Monday’s storm seem bigger to Kojo at first even though Wednesday brought more millimetres of rain?
Why do meteorologists empty the rain gauge at the exact same time every morning after recording the reading?
What is the difference between saying "It rained 18 mm on Wednesday" (weather) and saying "Southern Ghana has its major rainy season from April to July" (climate)?

If Saturday had 10 mm of rain, what would be the new total for all 6 days, and what would the 6-day mean be?

support: Use centimetre/millimetre rulers so learners can see how small 1 mm is (one-tenth of a centimetre) and mark 12 mm and 18 mm on paper strips.
stretch: Compare two weeks of rainfall data using a double bar chart and write three sentences comparing their totals and averages.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) operates synoptic and agro-meteorological weather stations across all regions of Ghana.
Akosua, Kojo, and Boateng are Akan names; Koforidua is the regional capital of the Eastern Region.
localiseThis: Discuss whether your school is in the southern bimodal rainfall zone (two wet seasons) or the northern unimodal rainfall zone (one wet season), and when farmers in your community plant maize, yam, or millet.

whatWeKnow: Rainfall depth is measured in millimetres using a standard funnel-and-cylinder rain gauge sited in an unobstructed open area.
Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions (hours to days), whereas climate describes statistical weather patterns over at least 30 years (WMO standard).
Ghana’s seasonal rainfall is driven by the north-south movement of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) / West African Monsoon.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Climate scientists at GMet and West African universities are studying how warming oceans in the Gulf of Guinea change the onset dates and intensity of extreme rainfalls for local farmers.

investigation.title: Build a Classroom Rain Gauge and Keep a 5-Day Log
materials: A clear, straight-sided 1.5-litre plastic bottle
Scissors (used by the teacher)
A handful of clean small pebbles or marbles
A plastic ruler marked in millimetres (mm) and waterproof tape
Water and a notebook
steps: Have the teacher cut the top curved shoulder off the plastic bottle (about one-third from the top).

Place a 3 cm layer of pebbles in the bottom of the bottle to weight it down so wind cannot tip it over, and pour water in just to the top of the pebbles—mark that flat water line as your "0 mm" starting line.
Tape a ruler vertically on the outside of the straight-sided bottle with the "0" mark aligned exactly with your starting water line, then invert the cut top into the bottle as a funnel.

Place the gauge in an open spot outdoors during a rainy week, read how many millimetres the water rises above the 0 line at 8:00 a.m. each morning, refill/reset to the 0 line, and draw a 5-day bar graph!
investigation.whatToNotice: Adding pebbles and filling water to a marked 0 line above the uneven bottle base gives a flat, straight-sided starting level so every millimetre of rain is measured accurately.
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should cut the plastic bottle and smooth any sharp plastic edges with tape; never go outside into an open field during active lightning or thunder—wait until the storm has passed to read the gauge.

factCheck.claim: A standard rain gauge measures precipitation depth in millimetres in an unobstructed open location, and climate is defined over a 30-year baseline.
factCheck.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) defines precipitation depth in mm (1 mm = 1 litre per square metre) and uses 30-year climatological standard normals to distinguish climate from daily weather.
factCheck.reference: World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8); Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) Educational Resources.
